title: The history of waves and resonance
tagline: From Pythagoras's strings to ripples in spacetime: how people learned that sound, light and even gravity travel as waves.
intro: Musicians knew for thousands of years that string lengths make harmony, but it took until the 1600s to see pitch as frequency and to write the laws of a vibrating string. Then came the speed of sound, patterns in sand, light's interference and Maxwell's discovery that light is an electromagnetic wave. The 20th century added radio, microwave ovens, a tabla explained by an Indian physicist, a bridge that twisted itself apart, and in 2015, waves in space itself.

eras.name: Strings and numbers
eras.summary: Harmony is found to follow whole numbers, the octave is split into equal steps, and Mersenne and Galileo tie pitch to frequency.

eras.name: Measuring sound
eras.summary: Sound needs air, pitch is counted in clicks, its speed is calculated and corrected, and sand reveals standing waves.

eras.name: Light becomes a wave
eras.summary: Young's fringes, Doppler's shifting pitch, Maxwell's equations and Hertz's radio waves show that light is an electromagnetic wave.

eras.name: Resonance at work
eras.summary: Drums explained, a bridge destroyed, kitchens transformed and gravitational waves detected.

events.title: Whole-number strings sound sweet
events.text: Greek tradition credits Pythagoras with finding that a string halved in length sounds an octave higher, and that lengths in ratios 3:2 and 4:3 give the fifth and fourth. The famous story of blacksmiths' hammers is a later legend and doesn't work physically.
events.why: It was the first law of nature written as numbers, and the seed of fₙ = n v ÷ 2L.

events.title: Twelve equal steps to the octave
events.text: The Chinese prince and scholar Zhu Zaiyu calculated how to split the octave into 12 equal steps, each the twelfth root of 2, about 1.0595 times the last, to many decimal places. Simon Stevin reached the same idea in Europe a few decades later.
events.why: Every modern piano key is tuned this way: each is 1.0595 times the frequency of the one below.

events.title: Mersenne's laws of strings
events.text: In Harmonie universelle, Mersenne set out how a string's pitch depends on its length (inversely), tension (as its square root) and weight per length (inversely as its square root). He also made the first absolute measurement of a note's frequency, about 84 vibrations a second.
events.why: These laws are v = √(T ÷ μ) and f = v ÷ 2L, the rules behind every stringed instrument.

events.title: Pitch is how fast it shakes
events.text: In Two New Sciences, Galileo argued that pitch is set by how many vibrations reach the ear each second, and compared vibrating strings with swinging pendulums, whose rhythm depends only on their length.
events.why: It tied musical pitch to frequency, and the pendulum's natural rhythm is exactly what a swing resonates with.

events.title: A bell in a vacuum
events.text: Using an air pump built with his assistant Robert Hooke, Boyle pumped the air from a glass jar holding a ticking watch. The ticking grew fainter as the air went and returned when it was let back in.
events.why: It showed that sound needs air to travel, while light passed through the empty jar untouched.

events.title: A wheel that sings a known pitch
events.text: Hooke held a card against a spinning toothed brass wheel. The faster it spun, the more clicks each second and the higher the note, so he could make a sound of known frequency on demand.
events.why: It showed directly that pitch is frequency, the idea behind every sound chapter since.

events.title: Newton calculates the speed of sound
events.text: In the Principia, Newton worked out the speed of sound from the springiness and density of air. He got about 298 m/s, some 15 % too low, and could not explain the gap.
events.why: It was the first attempt to predict a wave's speed from the medium it travels through, the idea that v is set by the medium, not the source.

events.title: Sand draws the nodes
events.text: Chladni scattered sand on metal plates and bowed their edges. The sand danced off the vibrating parts and gathered on the still lines, the nodes, making beautiful patterns that change with each note.
events.why: They made standing waves visible for the first time, and gave acoustics its founder.

events.title: Light makes interference fringes
events.text: In his 1801 Bakerian lecture Young explained colours by interference: waves that meet in step add, and waves out of step cancel. By 1803 he described light passing two slits and making bright and dark bands.
events.why: It was strong evidence that light is a wave, against Newton's popular idea of particles.

events.title: A prize for vibrating plates
events.text: Napoleon's Academy offered a prize for the mathematics of Chladni's patterns. Sophie Germain, a self-taught mathematician barred from universities as a woman, entered three times and won in 1816, the first woman to win a prize from the Paris Academy of Sciences.
events.why: Her work began the theory of elastic plates, still used to design everything from loudspeakers to bridges.

events.title: Laplace fixes Newton's error
events.text: Laplace realised that squeezed air in a sound wave warms up and stretched air cools, too fast for the heat to escape. Adding that effect raised Newton's speed of sound to match the measured value, about 340 m/s.
events.why: It closed a 130-year puzzle and is why the box uses v = 331 √(1 + T/273) m/s.

events.title: Moving sources change pitch
events.text: Doppler proposed that a wave's frequency depends on how its source and listener move: higher when approaching, lower when moving apart. In 1845 C. H. D. Buys Ballot tested it in the Netherlands with musicians playing a steady note on a moving train.
events.why: The Doppler effect now measures blood flow, weather and the expansion of the universe.

events.title: Light is an electromagnetic wave
events.text: In A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field, Maxwell showed that electric and magnetic fields can travel together as a wave. The speed his equations predicted matched the measured speed of light.
events.why: It joined light, electricity and magnetism, and predicted invisible waves nobody had yet made.

events.title: Hertz makes radio waves
events.text: With a spark gap and a loop of wire, Hertz sent and detected invisible electromagnetic waves across his lab. He reflected them off a metal sheet to make standing waves a few metres long, and showed they travel at the speed of light.
events.why: It proved Maxwell right and opened the way to radio, TV, Wi-Fi and microwave ovens. The unit of frequency is named after him.

events.title: Why the tabla sings in tune
events.who: C. V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar
events.text: Most drums make overtones that are out of tune with each other. Raman and Kumar showed in Nature that Indian drums like the tabla and mridangam give harmonic overtones, in a musical series like a string's, thanks to the loaded black patch on the drumhead.
events.why: It explained, with physics, a design Indian drum makers had perfected by ear over centuries.

events.title: Galloping Gertie falls
events.text: Four months after opening, the 853 m span twisted about 12 times a minute in a steady 64 km/h wind, until it tore apart and fell into Puget Sound. Film of the collapse became world famous.
events.why: Often called resonance, it was really aeroelastic flutter: the twisting deck made the wind push it harder, and bridges have been wind-tested ever since.

events.title: A melted chocolate bar
events.text: Working on radar magnetrons, Spencer noticed a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted. He tried popcorn and an egg next, and Raytheon patented microwave cooking in 1945.
events.why: It led to the microwave oven, whose 12 cm standing waves this box lets you watch.

events.title: The wobbly bridge
events.text: On opening day, thousands of walkers made London's new footbridge sway sideways by about 70 mm. People fell into step with the sway, which made it worse. It closed after two days and reopened in 2002 with 37 fluid dampers and 52 tuned mass dampers.
events.why: It showed that people can drive resonance too, and changed how footbridges are designed.

events.title: Waves in space itself
events.text: Two detectors caught a gravitational wave from two black holes merging 1.4 billion light-years away. It stretched the 4 km arms by a thousandth of a proton's width, chirping from 35 to 250 Hz in a fifth of a second.
events.why: Einstein's last untested prediction was confirmed, opening a new way to observe the universe; the leaders won the 2017 Nobel Prize.

people.name: Marin Mersenne
people.note: Wrote the laws of vibrating strings and first measured a note's frequency.

people.name: Zhu Zaiyu
people.note: First to calculate twelve-tone equal temperament precisely.

people.name: Robert Hooke
people.note: Built Boyle's air pump and made tones of known frequency with a toothed wheel.

people.name: Ernst Chladni
people.note: Made standing waves visible with sand on vibrating plates.

people.name: Sophie Germain
people.note: Won the Paris Academy's prize for the theory of vibrating plates in 1816.

people.name: Thomas Young
people.note: Showed interference of light, evidence that light is a wave.

people.name: James Clerk Maxwell
people.note: Showed that light is an electromagnetic wave.

people.name: Heinrich Hertz
people.note: First made and detected radio waves; the unit of frequency bears his name.

people.name: C. V. Raman
people.note: Explained why the tabla and mridangam have musical overtones.

series.title: Early estimates of the speed of sound in air
series.caption: Seventeenth-century measurements and Newton's calculation scattered widely around today's 343 m/s at 20 °C.

facts: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge's only death was a dog named Tubby, left in a car on the deck.
Hertz, asked what his radio waves were good for, reportedly said they were of no use whatsoever.
The LIGO signal stretched 4 km arms by about a thousandth of the width of a proton.
Every piano key is the twelfth root of 2, about 1.0595, times the frequency of the one below it.
A microwave oven's hot spots, about 6 cm apart, let you measure the speed of light with a bar of chocolate and a ruler.
